claims.text: Formation and uniform dispersion of a secondary phase akin to HCP enhances the creep resistance of an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating.
The as-deposited FCC/BCC coating lacks significant secondary precipitates.
A controlled HIP-like thermal treatment can induce formation of a secondary phase in the primary matrix.
The treatment-induced secondary phase forms through a limited eutectoid reaction or precipitation.
Creep is relevant under sustained loading at elevated service temperatures.
A treatment-induced secondary phase can be evenly dispersed in the matrix or concentrated at grain boundaries.
The secondary phase impedes dislocation glide.
The secondary phase impedes dislocation climb.
Impeded dislocation motion reduces the rate of creep deformation.
Treated coatings with a uniformly dispersed secondary phase should accumulate less creep strain than untreated coatings.
A grain-boundary-concentrated secondary phase may provide less creep resistance than a uniformly dispersed phase.
The untreated coating should have a higher creep rate because it lacks a dislocation-pinning secondary phase.
The beneficial effect is limited to temperatures and stresses below those that cause excessive phase coarsening or dissolution.
Excessive phase coarsening or dissolution causes additional microstructural degradation.
The optimal precipitate size, volume fraction, and spatial distribution are not yet known.
Failure to reduce creep strain despite confirmed secondary-phase formation would falsify the proposed precipitate-controlled creep-resistance mechanism.
Failure to observe a measurable association between the secondary phase and altered dislocation behavior would falsify the proposed mechanism.
